title: Pair-Density Wave from Doping an Altermagnetic Mott Insulator
authors: Shuai A. Chen, Qianqian Chen, Guangyu Yu, Zheng Zhu
abstract: Pair-density-wave (PDW) superconductivity is a state in which the superconducting order parameter modulates at a finite wavevector. Using large-scale density matrix renormalization group, we study the doped altermagnetic Mott insulator in the checkerboard $t$-$J$ model, where altermagnetic exchange anisotropy is encoded microscopically through anisotropic ferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor exchange. By mapping the ground-state phase diagram as a function of doping and altermagnetic anisotropy, mainly on six-leg cylinders, we identify a transition from a uniform $d$-wave superconducting regime with charge modulation to a PDW regime coexisting with stripe order. In the PDW regime, we report an unconventional wave-vector locking $\mathbf Q_{\mathrm{PDW}}\approx 2\mathbf Q_{\mathrm{Stripe}}$ along the cylinder direction, in contrast to the conventional relation. Pair correlations reveal a two-scale structure, consisting of short-distance local $d$-wave pairing and long-distance finite-momentum PDW correlations. A symmetry-based Ginzburg--Landau analysis is presented for the observed locking. Our results identify altermagnetism as a strong-coupling, microscopically grounded route to finite-momentum superconductivity in doped Mott insulators.
summary: The authors use DMRG simulations on a doped altermagnetic Mott insulator described by the $t$-$J$ model to study superconductivity. They find that doping stabilizes a Pair-Density Wave (PDW) state coexisting with charge stripes, characterized by an unconventional wavevector locking ($Q_{PDW} \approx 2 Q_{Stripe}$). This work establishes altermagnetism as a strong-coupling mechanism driving finite-momentum pairing in these correlated materials.
main_problem: The study investigates whether doping an altermagnetic Mott insulator can stabilize a Pair-Density Wave (PDW) superconducting state, and how this PDW coexists with charge stripe order.
main_result: The system transitions into a PDW regime exhibiting an unconventional wave-vector locking relation ($Q_{PDW} \approx 2 Q_{Stripe}$), confirming altermagnetism as a route to finite-momentum superconductivity.
method: Large-scale Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) simulations were employed on checkerboard lattices to map the ground-state phase diagram and analyze correlation functions.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using the $t$-$J$ model applied to a doped altermagnetic Mott insulator on a checkerboard lattice. The Hamiltonian incorporates bond-anisotropic exchange ($\propto \eta$) that microscopically realizes the altermagnetic sublattice relation.
key_observables: Pair correlator ($D_{\alpha eta}(r)$), structure factors for superconducting and charge order ($\left| F_{sc}(q) ight|$ and $\left| F_n(q) ight|$), and local hole density $n(x)$.
important_parameters: Hole doping ($\delta$) and altermagnetic anisotropy ($\eta$), with focus on the regime $0.6 \le \eta \le 0.8$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mapping the ground-state phase diagram using DMRG techniques, assuming the validity of the $t$-$J$ model description for the correlated state.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the checkerboard lattice structure and magnon dispersion related to AM anisotropy. Key results show pair correlations exhibiting a two-scale structure (short-range $d$-wave + long-range PDW) and confirm the unconventional locking relation ($Q_{PDW} \approx 2 Q_{Stripe}$) via structure factors.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by defining the physical model and methods, mapping the phase diagram as a function of doping and anisotropy, presenting evidence for the coexisting PDW/stripe order, and concluding with a symmetry-based Ginzburg--Landau analysis to establish the unconventional locking mechanism.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses superconductivity in strongly correlated electron systems (Mott insulators) using advanced numerical techniques (DMRG), providing insights into how magnetic anisotropy can fundamentally alter superconducting pairing symmetries and wavevectors.
